Nikita looked up from her plate. "You were asleep in the pram, Tejas. I'm the one who told you about it. I was nine."
Tejas opened his mouth, then shut it. He could still see the monkey's hand. But was that his picture, or Nikita's story, told so many times it had become his?

Nobody pushed. Zainab cleaned the knee, then opened the notes on her phone and typed his words with the date, before dinner and before Kiran's father came home and asked his own questions.
Later she heard Kiran tell his father, "I fell and Aarush laughed." She noticed the new part and didn't argue. She had the first one written down.

My name is Vijay, and I want to write down the ticket fight while it's fresh, because I nearly handled it badly.
Reena and I share a flat. In June we planned to go home for Diwali together, and last week we found no tickets booked. Reena said, "You said you'd book them." I felt the heat rise. I was sure she had said she would.

I felt my face go warm. I said sorry and booked the waiting-list seats. Reena laughed. "Good thing you checked before we started shouting."

Pooja and Uday disagreed in today's stand-up about the design deadline. Uday said everyone had agreed on the 12th. Pooja's shoulders went tight; she said she clearly remembered the 19th. The room went quiet.
What I noticed next: Pooja paused, then said, "That's how I remember it, anyway. I could be wrong. Let me check the meeting notes." She opened the shared file. The notes said the 19th, with Uday's initials next to it.
Uday went red, then laughed. "Okay, I'd have bet money on the 12th."
What struck me was how quickly the heat went out of the room once Pooja stopped saying "this is what happened".
What I did next: I asked everyone to add dates to the notes during meetings, not after, and I thanked Pooja in the group chat.

Sit, Pallavi. You're scrolling while the radio talks about the river, and it reminds me of something.
When I was sixteen, in Guwahati, I had my first phone. The river was rising and the evening news said low areas should move to higher ground. Our lane had never flooded, not once. I lay on the charpai playing a silly game and told your Nani, my mother, "It's just the news making drama."

Relief camp note, 14 August, 6:40 pm.
I reached the family's house in Bhatt Nagar lane at 5:15. The municipal van had announced evacuation at 4. Water was ankle-deep in the lane.
Chandrika ji, the mother, was wrapping steel plates in newspaper. Her son Zubin, about twenty, was taking down the wall clock and a box of certificates. He told me, calmly, "We'll be done in half an hour. It'll be down by morning anyway, it always is."
I said the river was faster this year. He nodded and carried on packing photo albums into a trunk. Twice he checked the lane and said it looked fine.
By 5:40 the water was at the doorstep. I asked him to leave the trunk. He looked at it for a long time, then picked up his grandmother instead and we walked out.
Next: I asked the team to reach this lane first tomorrow.

qa.q: What time had the municipal van announced evacuation?
qa.a: It had announced evacuation at 4.

qa.a: He felt calm and confident that the water would pass by morning, holding on to how things usually went.

Tuesday night, cousin's flat in Dehradun
Writing this with shaky hands. The landslide warning for our hillside came at two. Jeevan read it out. Papa said, "They say this every year." I agreed. Honestly, I was irritated. I had an assignment due.
We didn't leave. We started "getting ready". Mummy wanted the good bedsheets. I spent forty minutes choosing which books to take. Jeevan kept saying "Pooja, now, please," and I kept saying "Five minutes".
At 4:30 a stone the size of a football rolled onto the road below our gate. Then another. Then the sound, like a truck braking forever.
We left with half-zipped bags. The road was already cracking at one edge.
Everyone's fine. The house is fine too, for now. But I keep thinking of those forty minutes and how sure I felt.
Pooja

I'm Arohi, and I sit near the pantry on the fourth floor, so I saw the whole thing.
The fire alarm went off at 11:10, a loud, flat beep. Nobody stood up. Not one person. I watched heads lift, eyes slide to the next desk, then back down to screens. Someone near the window said, "Drill, probably." Someone else kept typing. I kept my hand on my mouse too, telling myself I'd move when the others did.
It went on for almost two minutes. Then Parul, from accounts, closed her laptop, stood, and said, "I'm going down." That was all.
Within seconds, chairs scraped everywhere. We filed down the stairs, a bit embarrassed. Out on the pavement, it turned out to be a real smoke alert from the ground-floor kitchen.

qa.a: Arohi could stand up and head for the stairs straight away, since one person moving is often what gets everyone else moving.

qa.a: She may have felt a little awkward being the first, but determined enough to act, and her move freed everyone else to follow.

Monday. The alarm shrieked across the open office. Jasleen looked at Noor, Noor looked at the manager, the manager looked at his screen. Nobody moved. Jasleen stayed seated too, heart thumping, and it stopped after a minute. Later they said it was a test.
Wednesday. At lunch, Jasleen asked Noor, "Why didn't we get up?"
Noor shrugged. "Nobody else did. I'd have felt silly."
"Me too. I was watching everyone watch everyone."
Friday, two weeks later. The alarm went off again during a call. Jasleen felt the same pull to look around. This time she said "Sorry, fire alarm" into her headset, stood, and walked to the stairs. Behind her she heard Noor's chair, then more chairs. Half the floor followed her down.

qa.a: Noor probably felt relieved to have someone to follow, since on Monday she stayed seated because she would have felt silly moving alone.

You're new here, Ira, so let me tell you about my first job, in a call centre in Pune. I was twenty-three.
One night the fire alarm went. Forty of us on headsets. I remember looking left: my team lead, still talking. Looking right: my friend Sunny, looking at me. Everyone was checking everyone else's face, like a room full of mirrors. So we all kept talking to customers in America while the alarm screamed.
Then Lakshmi akka, the woman who cleaned the floor at night, walked in with her bucket, looked at us all, and said in Marathi, "Are you all mad? Get out." She put the bucket down and held the door open.
We went. It was a small electrical fire in the server room. Not dangerous in the end. But I think of Lakshmi akka every time an alarm rings, Ira. I'm Deepika, and I get up first now.

qa.a: In a call centre in Pune.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi akka likely feeling when she said "Are you all mad?"
qa.a: She was probably alarmed and exasperated to see forty people ignoring a fire alarm.

qa.q: What choice inside the story broke the freeze, and why did it work?
qa.a: Lakshmi akka named the danger out loud and held the door open, which gave everyone a clear cue to leave instead of watching each other.

qa.q: How did Sunny seem to see the alarm while looking at Deepika?
qa.a: Sunny seemed unsure and was looking to Deepika for a cue, just as Deepika was looking at others.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague recalling how coworkers ignored a fire alarm, each watching the others, until one person moved.

The panchayat loudspeaker crackled just after lunch: the river upstream was rising, families near the ghat should move to the high school by evening.
Shreya had been teaching in the village for a year. She lived in two rooms near the ghat. The cloth bag she kept by the door already held a torch, a water bottle, her ID papers and a few biscuits. She picked it up, locked the school cupboard with the registers inside, and walked up the slope.
Tanvir, who ran the tea stall, laughed. "Madam, the river always talks and never comes."
"Then I'll have tea at the high school instead," she said, cheeks warm.
She sat on the steps there with three old women and a goat. By night the river had risen to the ghat's third step and stopped.
Tanvir brought her tea next morning. "So, madam. Nothing." She laughed with him.

Aiko always found the exits first. On her first night in the new flat in Sendai, before she unpacked, she walked the corridor to the stairwell and counted doors. Her small backpack with water, a torch and spare socks sat by the shoe rack.
Two weeks later her phone blared an earthquake alert while she and Mei were eating noodles. The floor rolled gently for a few seconds. Then a tsunami advisory came up for the coast.
"We're three kilometres inland," Mei said, still holding her chopsticks.
"The advisory says go up," Aiko said, already putting on her shoes.
They climbed to the school on the hill with the backpack and sat among families in blankets. Around midnight the advisory was lifted; the sea had risen only a little.
"All that for nothing," Mei said.
"I'd rather be a bit silly on a hill," Aiko said, a little red, and shared the torch.

qa.a: Water, a torch and spare socks.

Class 5B, observation note, Tuesday.
Santosh would not use the second-floor washroom today. He ran to the ground floor at break and was late back. When I asked, he said quietly that a woman in white appears in the mirror if you go alone.
I asked where he heard it. "Everyone says it, ma'am. Sabina's brother saw it." Sabina, sitting nearby, said her brother hadn't seen it, he had heard it from someone in Class 8.
Santosh looked confused. "But everybody knows it," he said, as though that settled it.
What I did next: I walked with Santosh and Sabina to the washroom, we switched on the light and looked at the mirror together. Tomorrow I'll talk with the class about how things feel true when we hear them many times.

qa.q: Which washroom would Santosh not use?
qa.a: He would not use the second-floor washroom.

qa.q: What does Santosh's reply "But everybody knows it" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt frightened and sure, because hearing the story over and over made it feel like a known fact.

qa.q: How does the note-writer's plan for tomorrow help?
qa.a: Talking with the class about how repeated stories feel true can help children question "facts" they only heard, instead of just fearing them.

qa.q: How does Sabina seem to see the story once she hears her brother's name?
qa.a: She seems to want to set it straight, pointing out that her brother only heard it from someone else and never saw it.

grounding: It shows a child believing a ghost "fact" because everyone repeats it, as noted by an adult who watched.
